summary: This standards-track RFC specifies the format and mechanism for encoding Access-Network Identifiers in DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 messages, by defining new Access-Network-Identifier options and sub-options.

plainLanguage.summary: A way for network equipment to stick a label on a request for network settings saying which access network it came through.

questions: what is the dhcp access network identifier option
what are dhcp option codes 105 to 110
what does a dhcp relay agent add for access network
what is dhcpv4 relay agent sub-option 13
subtitle: New DHCP options that let a relay agent tell the server which access network, access point and operator a client came through.

tldr.problem: In mobility deployments such as Proxy Mobile IPv6, the anchor needs to know which access network a device is attached to, so it can apply different service treatment and policy.
tldr.mechanism: A DHCP relay agent adds Access-Network-Identifier information to messages it forwards: sub-options 13 to 18 in the DHCPv4 Relay Agent Information option, and options 105 to 110 in DHCPv6 Relay-forward messages.
tldr.outcome: The options carry access technology type, network name, access point name and BSSID, and operator identifier and realm. They expose location-like data, so the RFC requires care in storing it and securing the path.

today: RFC 7839 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 3046 for DHCPv4 and on RFC 3315 for DHCPv6.

sections.title: Why Report the Access Network
sections.content:
Knowing the access network of a device has several uses. In a Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) domain, the Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) can give service treatment to a mobile node's traffic based on the access network it is attached to. For example, treatment may differ between a network owned by the home operator and one owned by a roaming partner, or between configured IEEE 802.11 SSIDs. Operators may also apply tariffs by location.

RFC 6757 already defines PMIPv6 options that carry this information from the Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) to the LMA. This document gives the MAG a way to learn it: the DHCP relay agent in the access network adds the information to DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 messages. The scope is between a DHCP relay agent and a mobile access gateway, typically run by the same operator. In the RFC's example, the relay is on the Wi-Fi access point and the DHCP server is on the MAG.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask for an address, the helper at the door writes down which door you came through, so the people inside can treat visitors from different doors differently.

sections.title: The Information Carried
sections.content:
The Access-Network Identifier (ANI) is built from several pieces, each its own sub-option or option:

  • Access-Technology-Type (ATT): how the client is connected, using values from the registry defined in RFC 5213. It has a reserved byte that senders MUST set to 0 and receivers MUST ignore.
  • Network-Name: the SSID for IEEE 802.11, the PLMN Identifier for 3GPP, or the ANI for 3GPP2. Encoded as UTF-8.
  • Access-Point-Name: identifies the specific access point device, for example the string form of its MAC address. Encoded as UTF-8.
  • Access-Point-BSSID: the 48-bit BSSID of the access point.
  • Operator-Identifier: the operator's Private Enterprise Number, in network byte order.
  • Operator-Realm: the operator's realm, such as EXAMPLE.COM.

For a PLMN Identifier, both the Mobile Country Code and Mobile Network Code MUST be three digits; a two-digit network code is preceded by a 0.
sections.plainLanguage: The label can say what kind of network it is, the network's name, which exact access point you used, and which company runs it.

sections.title: DHCPv4 Sub-options
sections.content:
In DHCPv4, relay agents place the ANI as sub-options inside the Relay Agent Information option from RFC 3046. Each sub-option is a code, a length and data. The codes come from the DHCP Relay Agent Sub-Option Codes registry and range from 13 to 18.

The Access-Technology-Type sub-option (13) has length 2: a reserved octet and the ATT octet. Network-Name (14), Access-Point-Name (15) and Operator-Realm (18) carry variable-length text. Access-Point-BSSID (16) has length 6. Operator-Identifier (17) is shown with length 4.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of the label is a little tag with a number saying what it is, how long it is, and then the actual text.

sections.title: DHCPv6 Options
sections.content:
In DHCPv6 the relay agent may add the same information as full options in Relay-forward messages when it forwards any client message to the server. The options are OPTION_ANI_ATT (105), OPTION_ANI_NETWORK_NAME (106), OPTION_ANI_AP_NAME (107), OPTION_ANI_AP_BSSID (108), OPTION_ANI_OPERATOR_ID (109) and OPTION_ANI_OPERATOR_REALM (110).

Their contents are defined to be the same as the matching DHCPv4 fields. The ATT option has an Option-Len of 2, with the reserved and ATT bytes as in DHCPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv6 version is the same label with the same pieces, just written in the IPv6 style of tags.

sections.title: Relay Agent and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A relay agent MAY include these items. If it includes any of the network name, access point name or access point BSSID, it MUST also include the Access-Technology-Type, in both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6.

A server that does not understand the options or sub-options ignores them only, as the base DHCP specifications require. If it does understand them, it MAY use them for address pool selection or policy decisions. It MUST ignore the ANI if the Access-Technology-Type is missing while a network name, access point name or BSSID is present, and process the rest of the message normally. The server SHOULD NOT store the information unless absolutely needed, and if it does, MUST delete it as quickly as possible to avoid exposure to an intruder. A DHCPv6 server SHOULD look for the options in the Relay-forward message, based on its configured policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper may add the label. Whoever reads it should ignore a label that is missing its first line, and should not keep it longer than needed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DHCP messages have no privacy protection, so an eavesdropper on the link between the server and the relay can learn access-network information. The authentication options for DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 (RFC 3118 and RFC 3315) are not in active use, so the RFC does not rely on them. Link-layer confidentiality and integrity protection SHOULD be used.

A rogue relay agent, or a client posing as one, could insert or overwrite incorrect ANI options. Blocking these options unless the relay is trusted is a perimeter defense; the RFC says the authentication sub-option for the DHCPv4 Relay-Agent-Information option (RFC 4030) SHOULD also be deployed, and servers SHOULD communicate with relay agents using IPsec. Where the information cannot be secured with IPsec or other protocols, administrators SHOULD disable the capability.
sections.plainLanguage: The label shows where you came from, so it should be kept private and only trusted helpers should be allowed to write it.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned DHCPv4 relay agent sub-option codes 13 through 18 and DHCPv6 option codes 105 through 110, as listed in the earlier sections.
sections.plainLanguage: The official number keepers gave each tag its own number so nobody mixes them up.
